title: "Working pipeline"
output:
  html_document:
    df_print: paged
---
## 1) Import data. 

Source data should have a column with speaker identifiers (e.g., usernames) and one with text (e.g., social media posts)

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
Sys.unsetenv("GITHUB_PAT")
devtools::install_github("davidemorselli/speakerlandscapes", force = TRUE)
library(speakerlandscapes)

data = read_csv2("raw_corpus.csv")
head(data)

```
## 2) Make data ready to build landscapes.

This creates a `speakers_text` object: a character vector in which the first token is the speaker name, prefixed by an identifying token (e.g. "agent"). Bigrams and trigrams are found in the text and replaced by single tokens (e.g., word1_word2).

```{r}

ready_data = prepare_data(data, 
                          speaker_id_column = "speaker", 
                          text_column = "text", 
                          speaker_identifier = "agent")

head(ready_data)

```

## 3) Make the embedding

Compute the embeddings from the `speakers_text` object.

```{r}
embedding = train_embedding_model(ready_data, 
                                  min_count = 1,  # Beware, min_count=1 is only for the example. It indicates the minimum frequency required for a token to be included in the vocabulary. A higher number is preferable.
                                  stopwords_language = "en")


```

```{r}
# Validate ! Validate ! Validate !
# check embeddign by exracting simialr words to seed words
library(word2vec)
similar_words = predict(embedding, c("natural","protest"), type = "nearest", top_n = 10)

similar_words

```

# 4) Make the speaker landscape.

This step uses UMAP to reduce the 250-dimension embedding to a more interpretable 2-dimension space and extract speaker vectors.

```{r}
landscape = make_speaker_landscapes(data = ready_data,
                                    embedding = embedding, 
                                    speaker_identifier = "agent",
                                    retain_threshold = 1,
                                    n_neighbors = 30,
                                    min_dist = 0.01) 


```

## 5) Plot the speaker landscape.

Plot the speaker landscape along with word tokens extracted using `get_most_frequent_tokens()`.

```{r}
frequent_words = get_most_frequent_tokens(ready_data, min_count = 10, stopwords_language = "en")

categories = data %>% 
  select(speaker, opinion) %>% 
  rename(author = speaker,
         categories = opinion) %>% 
  mutate(author = tolower(paste0("agent_", author)))

plot_speaker_landscapes(landscape,
                        tokens_to_plot = frequent_words,
                        alpha_points = .6, size_points = 1,
                        categories = categories)

```

## 6) Interactive landscape with click-to-view speaker texts

You can inspect what individual speakers said by clicking on their dots in an interactive visualization.
Use `plot_speaker_landscapes(..., interactive = TRUE)` or call `plot_interactive_landscape()` directly:

```{r}
# Click on any speaker dot to see their original texts in the inspector side panel
plot_speaker_landscapes(landscape,
                        tokens_to_plot = frequent_words,
                        categories = categories,
                        interactive = TRUE)
```

## 7) Coloring speakers by normalized cosine proximity to a dictionary centroid

You can project a thematic concept (e.g., anger, climate, optimism) into the embedding space by calculating the centroid of its dictionary tokens, and visualize speakers colored by their **cosine proximity** (where higher values = stronger alignment with the concept).

```{r}
# 1. Define a dictionary of concept tokens
anger_dict <- c("attack", "punish", "enemy", "harshly", "blackmail", "crush", "ridiculous", "arrogant")

# 2. Compute the dictionary centroid in embedding space
centroid <- compute_dictionary_centroid(anger_dict, embedding)


# 3. Plot colored by cosine proximity with custom legend title
plot_speaker_landscapes(landscape,
                         tokens_to_plot = anger_dict,
                         centroid = centroid,
                         embedding = embedding,
                         proximity_palette = c("lightyellow", "darkred"),
                         interactive = FALSE)
```

## 8) Extracting and plotting speaker clusters with HDBSCAN

You can identify density-based clusters of speakers on the 2D landscape using `extract_speaker_clusters()` (powered by `dbscan::hdbscan()`), and plot the clusters on the landscape. `minPts` (minimum size) is the parameter that controls how conservative or sensitive the clustering is to noise. It controls how clusters are formed and how much data gets thrown out as noise. High values (e.g., minPts = 10) are recommended in noisy datasets (like word embeddings or text) where you only want the most definitive clusters.

```{r}
# 1. Extract speaker clusters using HDBSCAN
landscape <- extract_speaker_clusters(landscape, minPts = 10)
landscape$clusters

# 2. Static landscape plot with cluster circles
plot_speaker_landscapes(landscape,
                        tokens_to_plot = frequent_words,
                        show_clusters = TRUE,
                        label_clusters = TRUE)
```


```{r, eval=FALSE}
# 3. Interactive landscape plot with cluster circles
plot_speaker_landscapes(landscape,
                          tokens_to_plot = frequent_words,
                          show_clusters = TRUE,
                          label_clusters = TRUE, 
                         interactive = TRUE)
```

## 9) Calculating proximity between cluster and dictionary centroids

You can measure how semantically aligned each speaker cluster is to a thematic dictionary concept (such as anger or climate tokens) using `calculate_cluster_centroid_proximity()` (or `calculate_cluster_centroid_distance()`). It shows you the cosine similarity and the Euclidean distance between the cluster centroide and the thematic concept.

```{r}
# Calculate normalized cosine proximity between cluster centroids and the anger dictionary centroid
cluster_proximity <- calculate_cluster_centroid_proximity(
  speaker_landscape = landscape,
  centroid = centroid,
  embedding = embedding,
  space = "both"
)

cluster_proximity %>% 
  select(cluster_label,n_speakers,cosine_similarity,dist_2d)
```
